n: Zion is told to wake up and dress in strength and beautiful clothes, because the unclean will no longer invade her. The Lord explained in D&C 113 that putting on strength means putting on the authority of the priesthood. This verse is quoted in 2 Nephi 8:24, 3 Nephi 20:36, and Moroni 10:31.

f.w: put on thy strength, O Zion

f.g: Those outside the covenant and those ritually impure—here, invaders who defiled the city.

n: Shake off the dust, rise and take your seat (on a throne), and slip off the slave collar from your neck. D&C 113:9-10 explains the bands as the curses of God, and the call as scattered Israel returning to the Lord.

f.w: loose thyself from the bands of thy neck

f.g: Sit enthroned, as a queen—no longer on the ground as a captive.

n: You sold yourselves for nothing, and you will be redeemed without money. Peter teaches that we were redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ.

f.w: ye shall be redeemed without money

n: History review: Israel once lived in Egypt as foreigners and was later oppressed by Assyria for no good reason.
Now again My people are taken away for nothing; their rulers make them wail, and My name is insulted every day. Paul quotes the last line about God’s name being blasphemed.

f.w: my name continually every day is blasphemed

n: Therefore My people will come to know My name—that I am the One speaking: “Here I am.” Jesus quoted this to the Nephites.

A beloved verse: how beautiful are the feet of the messenger running over the mountains with good news of peace and salvation, telling Zion, “Your God reigns!” Abinadi explained it as referring to prophets and especially to Christ, the bearer of good tidings.

f.w: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet

n: Zion’s watchmen sing together, seeing “eye to eye”—face to face, unmistakably—the Lord returning to Zion. Latter-day Saints also apply it to watchmen united in testimony.

f.w: they shall see eye to eye
f.g: Literally “eye in eye”—they will see directly, with their own eyes.

n: Jerusalem’s ruins are invited to burst into song together: the Lord has comforted and redeemed His people.
The Lord rolls up His sleeve, so to speak, baring His holy arm before all nations; the whole earth will see God’s salvation. Book of Mormon prophets quoted this repeatedly.

f.w: The LORD hath made bare his holy arm

n: Leave, leave! Don’t touch anything unclean. Those who carry the Lord’s holy vessels must be clean. Originally about priests bringing temple vessels back from Babylon, the Lord repeats this command in latter-day revelation.

f.w: be ye clean, that bear the vessels of the LORD

n: Unlike the first Exodus, which was hurried, this departure won’t be a panicked flight. The Lord goes in front and guards the rear—as with the pillar of cloud and fire.

f.w: ye shall not go out with haste

n: The fourth and greatest Servant Song begins (52:13–53:12). God’s servant will act wisely and succeed, and be lifted up and highly exalted.

Many were horrified at him—his appearance so disfigured he hardly looked human. Christians see the beaten, crucified Christ. In 3 Nephi 21:10 the Savior also speaks of a latter-day servant who would be “marred,” whom many Latter-day Saints associate with Joseph Smith.

He will “sprinkle” many nations—as a priest sprinkles blood or water to cleanse—and kings will be speechless, seeing what they had never been told. Paul applies the last part to preaching Christ to the Gentiles.

f.w: So shall he sprinkle many nations
f.g: Sprinkling was a priestly act of purification; some translate “startle.”

f.w: the kings shall shut their mouths at him
